records.sourceFile: Examination of the Impact of Substance Use on Sport Training and Competition in Collegiate Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Kowal I, Donohue B, Barchard KA, Kraus SW, Allen DN. Examination of the Impact of Substance Use on Sport Training and Competition in Collegiate Athletes. Sport Social Work Journal. 2025;Advance online publication.
paper.abstract: This methodological study developed and evaluated a four-item self-report measure of perceived alcohol- and illicit-drug interference with collegiate sport training and competition.
paper.tldr: The four-item measure showed good one-week stability and expected relationships with substance use and psychiatric symptoms. It may support confidential screening conversations, but it is not a diagnosis or an objective measure of performance loss.
paper.methods: A total of 285 NCAA, club, and intramural collegiate athletes completed the four interference items, validated psychiatric-symptom and substance-frequency measures, and demographic items. Reliability and construct relationships were evaluated; a selected subsample of 74 substance-using athletes interested in intervention also completed a structured diagnostic interview.
paper.findings: One-week test-retest reliability was good. Interference scores related positively to psychiatric symptoms, substance-use frequency, and age; males scored higher, while ethnicity and athlete type did not affect scores. In the 74-athlete subsample, higher scores among those with a current substance-use disorder were only a nonsignificant trend (p=0.08).
paper.limitations: The measure is self-reported and may be affected by stigma or perceived consequences. The diagnostic comparison used a small, selected intervention-interested subsample, and the study did not validate the score against objective training, competition, safety, or longitudinal outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: If used, embed the four questions in a confidential, supportive workflow with clear referral options and limits on data access. A positive response should prompt conversation and clinical assessment rather than automatic action.
paper.athleteDev: Normalize early, confidential help-seeking and explain how substance use can interact with sleep, mood, recovery, safety, and performance. Preserve athlete trust by separating care from discipline whenever policy permits.
paper.rtp: The score is not a clearance tool. Substance-related readiness decisions require clinical assessment of health, cognition, withdrawal or intoxication risk, treatment progress, and the demands and safety requirements of participation.

records.sourceFile: On the value of a premium college football player - Evaluating the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Losak JM, Posmanick BJ, Sauer RD. On the Value of a Premium College Football Player: Evaluating the Literature. Journal of Sports Economics. 2024;25(4):472-506.
paper.abstract: This sports-economics article reviewed and updated methods for estimating the marginal revenue product of premium college football players in a changing compensation environment.
paper.tldr: Top college football players appear to generate substantially more institutional value than historical cost-of-attendance compensation, but the exact gap is highly model-dependent. This is athlete-welfare context, not health or training evidence.
paper.methods: The authors reviewed foundational and contemporary marginal-revenue-product approaches and updated estimates using modern college-football revenue, draft-pick, team-performance, and institutional data. Alternative specifications included player-value measures and school and year fixed effects.
paper.findings: Across historical and updated approaches, premium players generated values materially above cost-of-attendance compensation. Conservative fixed-effect estimates still supported a substantial gap, while estimated magnitude changed with how player quality, team success, revenue, institutional stability, and endogeneity were handled.
paper.limitations: Marginal revenue product is sensitive to model specification, revenue-sharing and accounting choices, selection of premium-player proxies, and unmeasured program context. Fixed effects can absorb stable talent differences, causality remains uncertain, and the compensation and legal landscape continues to evolve.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the work to understand the institutional and welfare context surrounding collegiate athletes and resource conversations. Current compensation policy or individual valuation requires current legal, financial, and governance expertise beyond this paper.
paper.athleteDev: Recognize that financial treatment, role expectations, and perceived fairness can shape athlete trust and wellbeing. Keep those conversations distinct from judgments about commitment, health status, or training behavior.
paper.rtp: The paper provides no rehabilitation or clearance evidence. Financial or roster context should not alter clinical standards, privacy, informed consent, or an athlete-centered return-to-participation process.

records.sourceFile: Injury prevention in professional soccer players - Can re-warmup training be organized in the post-warmup and half-time during a soccer game in a short time.pdf

paper.citation: D'Onofrio R, Laterza F, Sannicandro I, Masucci M, Bovenzi A, Manzi V. Injury Prevention in Professional Soccer Players: Can Re-warmup Training Be Organized in the Post-warmup and Half-time During a Soccer Game in a Short Time? Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2024;64(9):950-957.
paper.abstract: This narrative review synthesized brief re-warm-up strategies that could fit the post-warm-up delay and halftime of professional soccer competition.
paper.tldr: Brief high-intensity activity can help preserve temperature and explosive readiness after passive match delays. The highlighted one-minute protocol is a practical template, not proof of injury prevention or a universal prescription.
paper.methods: The authors searched PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro, SPORTDiscus, and Google Scholar without a date limit and narratively synthesized 26 papers relevant to professional-soccer post-warm-up or halftime reactivation. The review emphasized strategies lasting less than approximately 90 seconds.
paper.findings: The review found that re-warm-up activity can mitigate decrements after passive rest. It highlighted one minute of high-intensity exercise near 90% VO2max that preserved sprint performance, muscle strength, and temperature and increased muscle activation without additional measured physiological or psychological fatigue.
paper.limitations: The review did not systematically grade certainty, and its concise one-minute recommendation rests on limited and heterogeneous evidence. Most outcomes were performance, temperature, or activation rather than match injury incidence, and feasibility depends on competition rules and space.
paper.practicalImplications: Build a rehearsed post-warm-up and halftime menu that preserves temperature and briefly restores explosive activity without creating fatigue. Test exact timing, modality, footwear, surface, staff roles, and substitute-specific options in the team's environment.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes why passive waiting can reduce readiness and give them a short, repeatable reactivation routine they can execute under bench and halftime constraints.
paper.rtp: Re-warm-up exposure can be progressed during reconditioning, but tolerance of one brief protocol is not clearance. Combine it with symptoms, capacity, football-specific exposure, and medical and performance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Muscle activity asymmetry of the lower limbs during sprinting in elite soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Pietraszewski P, Gołaś A, Matusiński A, Mrzygłód S, Mostowik A, Maszczyk A. Muscle Activity Asymmetry of the Lower Limbs During Sprinting in Elite Soccer Players. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2020;75:239-245.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study examined bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal EMG activity and side-to-side asymmetry during maximal sprinting in elite male soccer players.
paper.tldr: Hamstring and gluteal activation asymmetry related to 5-m and 30-m sprint time in a small elite-soccer sample. The measurements are descriptive and do not prove injury risk or that targeted activation work improves outcomes.
paper.methods: Sixteen elite male soccer players completed two maximal 30-m sprints separated by five minutes. Textile electrodes recorded bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal muscle-group activity, and regression analyses examined relationships between side-to-side average activation asymmetry and 5-m and 30-m sprint times.
paper.findings: Hamstring asymmetry had significant regression relationships with 5-m (p=0.044) and 30-m (p=0.045) times, and gluteal asymmetry with 5-m (p=0.044) and 30-m (p=0.043) times. The largest descriptive imbalance occurred in the gluteal group and the smallest in the quadriceps.
paper.limitations: Only 16 athletes were assessed in one session. Textile EMG samples broad muscle regions, external sprint mechanics and gastrocnemius and tibialis activity were not measured, and cross-sectional associations do not establish causation, injury risk, or a response to training.
paper.practicalImplications: When bilateral activation data are available, interpret them alongside sprint splits, technique, strength, symptoms, history, and repeated measurements. Program hamstring and gluteal work for demonstrated performance needs rather than an isolated percentage.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that some side-to-side difference is expected and task-dependent. Focus on producing effective sprint shapes and force while building both limbs, instead of chasing perfect EMG symmetry.
paper.rtp: A single EMG asymmetry result is not a reinjury or clearance marker. Use repeated sprint exposure, symptoms, strength and power, mechanics, and sport tolerance to judge progression.

records.sourceFile: Peak instantaneous PlayerLoad metrics highlight movement strategy deficits in professional male soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Mitchell A, Greig M. Peak Instantaneous PlayerLoad Metrics Highlight Movement Strategy Deficits in Professional Male Soccer Players. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024;32(1):61-71.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study tested whether mid-calf accelerometry adds movement-strategy information to multidirectional single-leg hop distance in professional male soccer players with and without previous injury.
paper.tldr: Previously injured players hopped less far and their affected limb reached peak mediolateral loading later, despite no consistent reduction in peak load. Accelerometry may add context to performance scores, but it is not an injury or readiness threshold.
paper.methods: Twenty-five professional male players from one English Championship club completed three anterior, medial, and lateral hops per limb in one familiarized session. Twelve were classified as not previously injured and 13 as previously injured; hop distance and planar peak instantaneous PlayerLoad magnitude and timing were analyzed by task, injury status, and limb dominance.
paper.findings: Task and previous injury affected hop distance (p<0.001), dominance did not, and no overall bilateral asymmetry was detected (p=0.668). Previously injured players did not consistently show lower peak loading, but time to peak mediolateral loading was longer in the affected limb (p=0.001), especially when the injury involved the nondominant limb.
paper.limitations: The small one-club sample combined different previous injuries and relied on retrospective history. Accelerometer PlayerLoad is a surrogate measured during one session, and no prospective injury, rehabilitation response, or return-to-sport outcome was tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Assess performance outcome and movement strategy together and inspect both limbs. If time-to-peak or planar loading differs, use the result to guide further clinical and biomechanical assessment rather than applying an automatic decision rule.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes that achieving hop distance can mask a changed landing strategy. Use the data to explain targeted landing and loading work without framing every difference as pathology.
paper.rtp: Accelerometry can complement a return-to-sport battery, particularly when both limbs and multiple directions are assessed. It cannot replace symptoms, force and capacity measures, running and change-of-direction exposure, or sport-specific progression.

records.sourceFile: Performance of Future Elite Players at The NFL Combine.pdf

paper.citation: Hedlund DP. Performance of Future Elite Players at the National Football League Scouting Combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018;32(11):3112-3118.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort analysis compared NFL Scouting Combine characteristics across position groups and later Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition.
paper.tldr: Combine characteristics differed between later award groups, but the patterns were position-specific and sometimes counterintuitive. The data provide descriptive context rather than a validated individual prediction model.
paper.methods: Secondary combine and NFL career data were compiled for 5,506 athletes who attended the combine and were drafted between 2002 and 2016. Height, mass, 40-yard dash, vertical jump, bench press, shuttle, and three-cone results were compared within eight position groups by later Pro Bowl and All-Pro status.
paper.findings: Awarded players differed from nonawarded players on selected physical measures, with the relevant direction and combination varying by position. Faster 40-yard performance was common across several elite groups, while body size, jumping, bench repetitions, shuttle, and three-cone patterns were not uniformly favorable across positions.
paper.limitations: The analysis excluded undrafted attendees and nonattendees, contained missing test data, and included active careers. Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition depends on voting, opportunity, team and role; many comparisons were made, and no out-of-sample individual prediction model was validated.
paper.practicalImplications: Use positional distributions to frame preparation and identify a prospect's development priorities while preserving football skill and health. Evaluate the whole player and the uncertainty around every test.
paper.athleteDev: Help prospects treat combine tests as trainable expressions within a larger football profile. Avoid unsafe mass change or overfitting preparation to a benchmark that does not guarantee a career outcome.
paper.rtp: Combine norms are not rehabilitation standards. A recovering athlete must first demonstrate tissue capacity, football-specific exposure, and safe test readiness before maximal showcase preparation.

records.sourceFile: Effects of chronic static stretching interventions on jumping and sprinting performance - A systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Warneke K, Freundorfer P, Plöschberger G, Behm DG, Konrad A, Schmidt T. Effects of Chronic Static Stretching Interventions on Jumping and Sprinting Performance: A Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2024;15:1372689.
paper.abstract: This systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis evaluated whether chronic static-stretching programs improve jumping and sprinting performance.
paper.tldr: Chronic static stretching produced only a trivial pooled jump improvement and no significant sprint effect. It may serve mobility goals but should not displace sprint, plyometric, or resistance training for performance development.
paper.methods: Fourteen studies identified through PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar contributed 29 effect sizes: 20 jump and nine sprint outcomes. Multilevel models pooled dependent effects, and jump subgroups were analyzed by stretch-shortening-cycle characteristics.
paper.findings: Six of 20 jump tests and six of nine sprint tests were individually positive, while two studies reported negative adaptations. The pooled jump effect was positive but trivial (effect size 0.16, p=0.04), jump subgroup effects were nonsignificant (p=0.09-0.44), and the sprint effect was nonsignificant (p=0.08).
paper.limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous in population, stretching intensity, weekly volume, duration, comparator, and outcome. Positive individual tests did not create consistent subgroup effects, and the review could not identify a performance-enhancing dose.
paper.practicalImplications: Program static stretching for a demonstrated range-of-motion need, tolerance, or preference. If sprint and jump development is the priority, retain direct high-velocity, plyometric, and strength stimuli and monitor whether stretching volume competes with them.
paper.athleteDev: Set the expectation that flexibility work can improve motion without automatically making an athlete faster or more explosive. Match the tool to the goal and track the outcome that matters.
paper.rtp: Static stretching may support graded range of motion, but it is not evidence of restored tissue capacity or explosive readiness. Progress loading and sport exposure independently.

records.sourceFile: Effects of combined uphill-downhill sprinting vs resisted sprinting methods on sprint performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Hamad MJ, Alcaraz PE, Sáez de Villarreal E. Effects of Combined Uphill-Downhill Sprinting Versus Resisted Sprinting Methods on Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(1):185-202.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared combined uphill-downhill and resisted-sprint interventions with traditional sprint training.
paper.tldr: Combined uphill-downhill training had a small pooled advantage over traditional sprinting, while resisted sprinting did not. The hill evidence was sparse and did not test early acceleration, so superiority remains uncertain.
paper.methods: Twenty-two studies yielded 24 eligible groups completing at least four weeks of training with a traditional-sprint control: six combined uphill-downhill and 18 resisted-sprint groups. Random-effects standardized mean differences compared pre-post sprint performance changes between intervention and control groups.
paper.findings: Combined uphill-downhill training modestly outperformed traditional sprinting (SMD -0.41, 95% CI -0.79 to -0.03; p=0.03). Resisted sprinting did not significantly outperform traditional sprinting (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.07; p=0.19), although both approaches improved from baseline.
paper.limitations: Only six uphill-downhill groups were included, five involved nonprofessional participants, and none tested sprint distances below 35 m. Slopes, resistance loads, populations, and tests varied, and sparse data limited subgroup and meta-regression confidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Combined hill sprinting can be considered when a safe, consistent surface is available and the goal includes later acceleration or maximum-speed exposure. Compare it with simpler sprint options using actual athlete splits and technical response.
paper.athleteDev: Teach how uphill and downhill segments change force and velocity demands. Introduce downhill exposure gradually and prioritize control and surface safety over chasing overspeed.
paper.rtp: Hill and resisted sprinting are loading tools, not clearance tests. Progress slope, speed, resistance, and total distance only after appropriate running capacity and symptom response are established.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Post-Exercise Heat Exposure on Acute Recovery and Training-Induced Performance Adaptations - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Ahokas EK, Hennessy RS, Hanstock HG, Kyröläinen H, Ihalainen JK. Effects of Post-Exercise Heat Exposure on Acute Recovery and Training-Induced Performance Adaptations: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:106.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined the acute recovery and longer-term performance effects of whole-body heat exposure applied after exercise in healthy adults.
paper.tldr: Post-exercise sauna or hot-water immersion produced mixed acute recovery findings and limited, mode-specific chronic benefits. Heat is an additional stressor and should be prescribed for a defined goal with hydration and safety controls.
paper.methods: Fourteen randomized or crossover studies with 194 participants compared whole-body post-exercise heat of at least 36°C with passive or placebo recovery. Nine assessed acute performance recovery and five repeated exposure alongside training; risk of bias was evaluated, but design heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Among acute studies, four found no performance effect, four a benefit, and one an adverse effect. Repeated heating may have improved running performance, particularly in hot conditions, but did not improve cycling performance or VO2max. Overall evidence quality was low to moderate.
paper.limitations: Samples were small and heat modality, temperature, duration, exercise, outcome, recovery interval, and training status varied markedly. Too few comparable studies were available for pooling, so no definitive recovery or adaptation effect can be estimated.
paper.practicalImplications: State the purpose before adding heat: recovery, heat acclimation, or a training stimulus require different protocols. Screen medical risk, control hydration and supervision, and monitor the athlete's next-session performance and perceived recovery.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that feeling relaxed after heat does not prove physiological recovery. Athletes should report dizziness, excessive fatigue, illness, or hydration problems and should not use heat to compensate for poor sleep or nutrition.
paper.rtp: Heat may increase cardiovascular and hydration strain during rehabilitation. Introduce it only when clinically appropriate and never interpret tolerance of a sauna or hot bath as evidence of tissue or sport readiness.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Resisted-Sprint Training on Sprint Performance and Mechanics - A Systematic Review and Meta-AnalysisFocusing on Load Magnitude.pdf

paper.citation: Xu K, Jukic I, Cross MR, Hicks DS, Yin M, Zhong Y, Tang W, Li Y, Liang Z, Wang R, Morin JB, Girard O. Effects of Resisted-Sprint Training on Sprint Performance and Mechanics: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Focusing on Load Magnitude. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025;35:e70182.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined resisted-sprint load magnitude, sprint performance, and macroscopic sprint mechanics across direct and network comparisons.
paper.tldr: Resisted sprinting modestly outperformed unresisted sprinting overall, mainly for early acceleration, with selected advantages at moderate and very heavy loads. High bias and uneven evidence make the reported load threshold a hypothesis, not a universal prescription.
paper.methods: Forty-nine longitudinal studies involving 1,281 participants were analyzed with single-arm exploratory, direct two-arm, multilevel, and Bayesian network models. Loads were classified by body-mass percentage or velocity decrement, moderators were explored, and certainty was graded.
paper.findings: Resisted sprinting outperformed unresisted sprinting by Hedges' g -0.30 with moderate certainty. Moderate and very heavy categories, but not light or heavy categories, showed advantages; very heavy loads outperformed light loads in selected models and improved theoretical force and power metrics. Benefits were largely driven by 0-5-m acceleration.
paper.limitations: Randomized studies were rated high risk of bias and many nonrandomized studies serious risk. Load categories, training volumes, and mechanical outcomes were uneven, female representation was low, and the 20.7% body-mass meta-regression threshold is not a prospectively validated cutoff.
paper.practicalImplications: Prescribe sled resistance from the targeted sprint phase and measured velocity decrement, then verify posture, contact strategy, distance, and adaptation. Heavier work can be useful for trained athletes, but maintain unresisted acceleration and maximum-speed exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Connect sled load to a clear purpose rather than a heavier-is-better mindset. Athletes should understand the acceptable velocity loss and technical standard for each rep.
paper.rtp: Resisted sprinting can grade horizontal force demand, but load categories are not injury-specific progression criteria. Advance resistance, speed, and free sprinting according to symptoms, mechanics, tissue capacity, and total exposure.

records.sourceFile: Effects of sleep deprivation on sports performance and perceived exertion in athletes and non-athletes -A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Kong Y, Yu B, Guan G, Wang Y, He H. Effects of Sleep Deprivation on Sports Performance and Perceived Exertion in Athletes and Non-athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2025;16:1544286.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized and crossover evidence on sleep deprivation, performance, and perceived exertion in athletes and healthy nonathletes.
paper.tldr: Sleep deprivation impaired multiple athlete performance domains and increased perceived exertion. The direction is actionable, but heterogeneous protocols and sparse subgroups do not provide a precise decrement for an individual athlete.
paper.methods: Forty-five randomized controlled or randomized-crossover studies identified through five databases to September 2024 were synthesized. Outcomes included aerobic and anaerobic endurance, explosive power, maximum force, speed, skill control, and perceived exertion, with subgroup analyses by population, deprivation type, and test time.
paper.findings: Athlete performance declined for aerobic endurance (SMD -0.66), explosive power (-0.63), maximum force (-0.35), speed (-0.52), and skill control (-0.87), while perceived exertion increased (0.39). Healthy nonathletes also had lower aerobic endurance, and several early- or late-partial-deprivation and afternoon subgroups were adverse.
paper.limitations: Studies varied in sleep manipulation, baseline sleep control, population, outcome, and bias. Some subgroups were small, female participation was insufficient for sex analysis, and multiple subgroup tests make exact timing and deprivation-type estimates less certain than the overall direction.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect sleep before demanding aerobic, strength, speed, skill, and decision-heavy work. After verified loss, consider reducing complexity or dose, increasing monitoring, and rescheduling high-consequence assessment where feasible.
paper.athleteDev: Build a travel and disruption plan that emphasizes honest reporting, consistent sleep opportunity, and coordinated training adjustments. Discourage reckless stimulant use or extra training intended to compensate for fatigue.
paper.rtp: Sleep loss can depress rehabilitation and testing performance without reflecting tissue capacity. Interpret a poor session cautiously, address safety and cognition, and repeat high-stakes testing under representative recovery when possible.

records.sourceFile: Efficacy of heavy eccentric calf training for treating mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy- a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Murphy MC, Travers MJ, Chivers P, Debenham JR, Docking SI, Rio EK, Gibson W. Efficacy of Heavy Eccentric Calf Training for Treating Mid-portion Achilles Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(17):1070-1077.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared heavy eccentric calf training with natural history, traditional physiotherapy, and other exercise for chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.
paper.tldr: Heavy eccentric calf training was better than passive or traditional-physiotherapy comparisons in low-certainty evidence but was not better than other progressive exercise. It is one loading option, not a mandatory gold-standard protocol.
paper.methods: Seven randomized trials with 241 adults who had mid-portion Achilles symptoms for more than three months were included. Pain and function were measured with VISA-A, risk of bias and evidence quality were assessed, and pooled comparisons were made against natural history, traditional physiotherapy, and other exercise.
paper.findings: VISA-A favored heavy eccentric training over natural history by 20.6 points (one study) and traditional physiotherapy by 17.70 points (two studies). Against other exercise, the pooled difference was nonsignificant; after removing one high-risk study, other exercise was favored by 5.65 points, a difference judged unlikely to be clinically important.
paper.limitations: All studies were small and evidence was low or very low quality. Participants were generally middle-aged with longstanding symptoms, exercise protocols and adherence varied, and there were too few studies to assess publication bias or confidently generalize to younger competitive athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Select eccentric, heavy-slow, or other progressive calf loading according to athlete tolerance, access, adherence, and the force-speed demands being restored. Monitor symptoms and function and integrate running, plyometrics, and sport exposure rather than relying on one exercise recipe.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that tendon rehabilitation requires progressive loading and patience, but one famous protocol is not the only route. Choose a sustainable program and track meaningful function rather than soreness alone.
paper.rtp: VISA-A improvement and calf loading are components of rehabilitation, not clearance by themselves. Progress return to running and sport using symptoms, plantar-flexor capacity, elastic tasks, repeated exposure, and sport-specific demands.
